description: Temp0.7 is a club of three friends in software-related majors, and Space Apps 2026 Seoul is our first official activity. Our name comes from LLM temperature: 0.7 balances creativity and consistency. We work the same way, bold ideas that never lose direction. None of us is a doctor, so we set out to help non-experts monitor their own health and act in an emergency. We shared every role and asked of each step: is it backed by a public source, and can a frightened novice follow it?
summary: Orbit Guide is a web app that helps astronauts without medical training look after themselves and each other when Earth is minutes away. NASA already knows how the body changes in space, but that knowledge is written for doctors on Earth. On a Moon or Mars mission the first responder is a crewmate, up to 20 minutes from the nearest flight surgeon. Orbit Guide is the bridge. A 3D body shows each crew member's health against their own normal, in plain words, with what to do now. A daily check-in can be filled by hand or from a wearable. When a crewmate turns Urgent, a large alert names who needs help and opens one of 11 step-by-step emergency guides written for the helper, with voice cues and offline hands-free commands. Every reading and step becomes a timed log for the flight surgeon, sent with the real signal delay shown, and replies wait in an Earth inbox. All crew data is simulated, and every limit links to its NASA or clinical source. If it works 20 minutes from Earth, it can help anyone far from a doctor on Earth.
details:
What it does and how it works. NASA already knows how the human body changes in space, but that knowledge is written for doctors on Earth. On a Moon or Mars mission a message can take up to 20 minutes each way, and care starts with a crewmate who may not be a physician. Orbit Guide is a web app that connects existing NASA knowledge to that person through three bridges:

  1. Knowledge → person. A 3D body shows six body systems in four levels (Normal, Watch, Act, Urgent). Each value is judged two ways: against the crew member's own normal from mission days 1–14, and against fixed clinical and NASA limits. Tapping a part shows today's numbers, a small bar of where today sits in the personal range, a trend and what to do now. A daily check-in says what to measure and how, and can be filled by hand or from a (simulated) wearable.
  2. Person → person. When a crewmate's own readings turn Urgent, a large alert in the middle of every screen says who needs help and why; if it is closed, a red chip stays in the header until help starts. One tap opens 11 step-by-step emergency guides written for the helper ("Tap Kim's shoulders…"). CPR starts at once with a 110-per-minute beat and 2-minute swap alerts. Measure steps can be filled from the patient's wearable, and every reading goes into the patient's record. Voice cues read the steps aloud, and offline hands-free commands ("Start", "Next", "Yes", "No", "Back", "Stop") help when both hands are busy.
  3. Space → Earth. Every reading and step becomes a T+ timed log with patient, responder and the patient's usual range, sent to the flight surgeon with the real signal delay shown. The (simulated) reply names what was received and asks for the next piece of information that guide needs, and all messages wait in an Earth inbox.

Benefits. Earlier warning from a personal baseline, a clear first step for a non-doctor under stress, and a complete, timed record for the flight surgeon.

Intended impact. The same gap exists on Earth: the WHO and World Bank report that half of the world's people lack full access to essential health services. Antarctic stations, ships, remote villages and disaster zones could use the same app by changing only the delay setting, the limits table and the guide list.

Tools and languages. HTML, CSS and JavaScript in one page with no install or server; three.js (MIT) for the 3D body; Vosk speech recognition (Apache-2.0) bundled for offline commands; the browser's Web Speech API for spoken cues; GitHub Pages for hosting. All data comes from one function, so real sensor data can replace the simulation later. Six mission settings (ISS, Gateway, Moon base, lunar rover, Mars transit, Mars base) each carry their own signal delay, radiation dose, gravity and cabin CO₂.

What is creative about it. We did not try to invent new sensors or medicine. The new part is the bridge: grading against each person's own normal as well as textbook limits, emergency guides written for the helper rather than the patient, and an Earth log built around a 20-minute delay instead of a live call.

Factors we considered. A frightened non-doctor: one step per screen, big buttons, plain words, color plus words and never color alone. Busy hands: voice cues and hands-free commands. Real failures: a guide in progress survives a crash, timers keep running in the background, any step can be undone and the log keeps every entry. No network: the page works offline once loaded. Two languages: English and Korean.

Limits we state openly. All crew data is simulated; real astronaut medical data needs data-use agreements. Thresholds come from public references, and the personal-baseline rules are our own design. Emergency guides are example procedures that support, never replace, the onboard checklist and the flight surgeon. It is not a medical device. Source code: https://github.com/Painless-Bot/Nasa_Temp0.7
